articles.title: FOURTEEN PERSEIDS
articles.summary: This article, titled "FOURTEEN PERSEIDS," compiles multiple mini-reports on the Perseid meteor shower, highlighting the varied experiences of different observers. While some like Jack Zalders at Fremont Peak observed significant activity, including fireballs and lingering trains, others like Jay Freeman at Palo Alto Baylands saw very few meteors. The piece emphasizes the fragmented nature of observing events and also includes a calendar of upcoming astronomy events for September and October, such as star parties and classes.

articles.title: THE SEARCH FOR THE COSMIC WOBBLE
articles.summary: Journalist Jon Carroll recounts his private tour of Lick Observatory with astronomer Geoff Marcy, expressing his long-held fascination with observatories. The article describes their afternoon chat and a visit to the historic 108-year-old telescope, with the broader topic hinted at by the title, "THE SEARCH FOR THE COSMIC WOBBLE."

articles.title: Perseids, from p. 1
articles.summary: This article compiles diverse personal accounts of observing the Perseid meteor shower, primarily in August 1997. Observers reported a wide range of experiences, from successful sightings of dozens or hundreds of meteors in dark locations, sometimes including bright fireballs and 'mini-storms,' to complete disappointment due to clouds, light pollution, or poor timing. The collection highlights both the thrill of astronomical observation and the challenges posed by weather and urban environments.

articles.title: Cosmic Wobble, from p. 1
articles.summary: The article recounts a visit to the Lick telescope, offering a glimpse into the life of the observatory community and the 'romance of science.' The author details an encounter with astronomers Geoff Marcy and Paul Butler, highlighting their groundbreaking discovery of exoplanets by observing the gravitational 'wobble' of stars, a feat that transformed our understanding of planetary systems beyond our own sun. It emphasizes the perseverance required for scientific discovery despite initial skepticism.

articles.title: Bill Arnett
articles.summary: SJAA members attempted to observe an Aldebaran graze near Gilroy but missed the event due to clouds and the low position of the Moon and Aldebaran above the eastern horizon. Although they missed the main event by ten minutes, they still enjoyed viewing Jupiter and considered it a nice night under the stars.

articles.title: Rich Neuschaefer
articles.summary: Rich Neuschaefer discusses the ideal size for a single refractor telescope, weighing the merits of four-inch, five-inch, and six-inch models based on portability, lunar/planetary detail, and deep-sky performance. He also explores the significant differences between achromatic and apochromatic refractors, focusing on false color, contrast, and cost considerations to guide amateur astronomers in their equipment choices.

articles.title: George Zay
articles.summary: The article describes the Alpha Aurigids meteor shower, which becomes active after the Perseids. While generally low in rates, it features a sharp peak on the morning of September 1st, where observers in dark skies may see up to 50 bright meteors with long-lasting trains, radiating from Auriga. The shower is potentially linked to particles from Comet Kiess.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: This section, titled 'ASTRO ADS,' serves as a classifieds board for astronomically related products. It lists used equipment for sale, such as an encoder package, an Edmund Astroscan, and a refractor. The document also provides guidelines for submitting free noncommercial ads, including contact information for the editor and details on ad duration.

articles.title: Don Machholz
articles.summary: This article provides an update on several comets, highlighting the recent discovery of Comet Tilbrook and detailed viewing predictions for Comet Hale-Bopp for Northern Hemisphere observers, noting its changing position and optimal viewing times. It also briefly mentions the potential fading of Comet Tabur, new SOHO satellite discoveries, and statistics on the extensive efforts involved in comet hunting by other astronomers.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: The article presents a detailed table of orbital elements for three celestial objects: Hale-Bopp, Tabur, and Tilbrook. It provides key astronomical data such as perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period for each object. The data also includes reference sources, epoch dates, and absolute magnitudes.

articles.title: Ephemerides (for 0h UT)
articles.summary: This document provides detailed ephemerides for three comets: C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp), C/1997 N1 (Tabur), and C/1997 O1 (Tilbrook). For dates between August and October, each table lists the comet's celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), elevation, observed sky conditions (Morning or Evening), and apparent magnitude at 0h UT, serving as a guide for observers.

articles.title: Lunar Phases
articles.summary: This document provides a tabular overview of lunar phases, including New Moon (N/M), First Quarter (FQ), Full Moon (FM), and Last Quarter (LQ) for a given month. For each phase, it lists the precise time and date, along with the moonrise and moonset/sunset times. The data serves as a quick reference for celestial events related to the Moon's cycle.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides observational data for the planet Mercury, including its distance from the Sun (0.95 A.U.) and apparent magnitude (-2.3). It features a table detailing its rise, transit, and set times, as well as its right ascension and declination for three dates within a given month. This information is essential for astronomers and observers looking to locate and track Mercury.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This document provides current ephemeris data for Venus, including its distance from the Sun (A.U.) and apparent magnitude. It lists specific rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination coordinates for three different dates, aiding in locating the planet in the sky.

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for the planet Mars, detailing its astronomical data over a period. It includes Mars's distance in A.U., visual magnitude, and a table of rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination for three specific dates.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides astronomical ephemeris data for Jupiter for three dates within a month, including its rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension (R.A.) and Declination (Dec.). It also lists Jupiter's approximate distance at 4.25 Astronomical Units (A.U.) and its visual magnitude at -2.7.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides astronomical data for Saturn, detailing its magnitude, distance, and ephemeris including rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension and declination for specific dates. It also includes similar data for a celestial body or reference point labeled "SOL Star Type GZV," indicating its ephemeris and 'Hours of Darkness' over a period.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document presents a table detailing the start and end times of astronomical twilight for three specific Julian Dates: September 7, 17, and 27, 1997. The data illustrates the daily variation in astronomical twilight duration across these dates.

articles.title: Siderealtime
articles.summary: The article 'Siderealtime' presents a table showing the 'Transit Right Ascension at Local Midnight' for three different dates (07, 17, 27). For each date, it indicates the local time corresponding to 00:00 sidereal time. This data is relevant for understanding or utilizing sidereal time in astronomical contexts.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night
articles.summary: This brief entry, titled "Darkest Saturday Night" for a placeholder date of "00-Sept-97", lists key astronomical times such as sunset, twilight end, moonset, and dawn begin. Despite the use of placeholder data, it appears to be a schedule or planning note for an astronomical observing session prioritizing optimal darkness.

articles.title: ACTIVITIES THROUGH OTHER CLUBS
articles.summary: TAC has successfully reserved the Montebello site for use every Wednesday indefinitely, providing a consistent and accessible location for astronomy enthusiasts. This ongoing arrangement allows individuals to plan ahead and enjoy company at the nearby site, a unique offering in the astronomical community.

articles.title: September
articles.summary: This document outlines a series of astronomical events scheduled for September, including a General Meeting with an equipment night, multiple public observing sessions at different locations like Van Meter School and Grant Ranch, and a dedicated lunar observing session. These appear to be activities organized by amateur astronomy clubs like PAS, TAC, and FPOA.

articles.title: October
articles.summary: This document outlines two upcoming astronomical events for October: a public night on the 10th at TAC Van Meter School and lunar observing on the 11th at FP or Henry Coe. It also provides contact details for SJAA news and information, including a hotline, website, and instructions for subscribing to their mailing list.

articles.title: DIRECTIONS TO SJAA PLACES
articles.summary: This document provides detailed driving directions to three key locations used by the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA): Houge Park in San Jose, Henry Coe State Park near Morgan Hill, and Fremont Peak State Park south of San Juan Bautista. It outlines routes from major highways like Hwy 17, Hwy 85, and Hwy 101, and mentions any associated entrance fees for the state parks.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current Officers and Board of Directors for an organization. It provides the names and associated phone numbers for key leadership roles including President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and several Directors.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document lists the staff members for the "Ephemeris" publication, detailing their roles and contact information. It includes the Editor, Circulation contacts, and Layout designer along with their respective phone numbers.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Program Status
articles.summary: This document provides a status update for a telescope loaner program, detailing various telescopes, their current borrowers, and due dates. It indicates which telescopes are available for loan to any SJAA member. Contact information for reservations is also provided.

articles.title: Submit
articles.summary: Members of the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) are encouraged to submit articles for publication in their monthly newsletter, the *SJAA Ephemeris*. Submissions, including name and phone number, should be emailed to Dave North by the tenth of the month to appear in the following issue.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) membership form, detailing standard and junior membership fees, and an optional Sky & Telescope subscription. It provides instructions for submitting the form and payment, either by mail to the treasurer or in person at an SJAA meeting, along with necessary contact information and the association's address.
